body: Vectors refreshed: V3 keyset vector 1 now has keys 1 to 8 (new id `022546ab...`), so every keyset-derived value in tests/00, 13 and 29 changed; proofs carry real signatures, request outputs are distinct, the partial mint and a new melt-with-change vector show the mint's blind signatures, and 02-tests gains a v3 auth keyset (vector 4).
Rebuilt as cashubtc/nuts#469 (legacy/ is now main's files unchanged, root is v3 plus the mixed-keyset interop). Closing this one.

Could this cover payment requests before it merges? The fountain layer carries opaque bytes, but the Cashu mapping is tokens only: `M` MUST be the `crawB` token and the receiver MUST validate that envelope. So a request sent as frames is non-conforming today, and requests do outgrow a static QR once a merchant adds transports and a lock.

Some sizes from cashu-ts (QR level M, frames at 183 byte fragments):

| Request | `creqb` chars | Static QR | TLV bytes | Frames |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P2P: 1 mint, nostr, description | 323 | v11 | 194 | 2 |
| Shop: 2 mints, nostr + POST, 2 methods, single-key lock | 822 | v19 | 506 | 3 |
| Same shop request with a 2-of-3 lock | none | n/a | 774 | 5 |

The last row has no `creqb` form at all: it would be 1251 characters, and bech32m's code length is 1023. Only the key policy differs from the row above: the lock is written as nutroot plus the `nut10` copy for payers that predate v3, and three keys in both forms take it past the limit. cashu-ts refuses to encode it and, from reading rust-bech32, I think CDK does too.

One option is a second mapping alongside the token one, eg `M = UTF8("creqB") || TLV(PaymentRequest)` using the NUT-26 TLV bytes, with receivers dispatching on the five-byte prefix after reconstruction. Raw TLV keeps the saving this PR already made for tokens by dropping the text layer. The prefix name is a strawman. Happy to add test vectors if useful, and I have it sketched in cashu-ts.

Some numbers from testing this against UR, in case they are useful. Mac screen as sender, iPhone as receiver, 8 fps, 183 byte fragments, sample tokens with DLEQ proofs. UR is bc-ur 1.1.12 as cashu.me uses it, at the same fragment setting.

| Token | Format | Fragments | Frames read | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 proofs (~3,650 chars) | Fountain | 15 | 16 | 1.9 s |
| 12 proofs | UR | 20 | 31 | 3.7 s |
| 40 proofs (~11,900 chars) | Fountain | 49 | 49 | 6.0 s |
| 40 proofs | UR | 66 | 96 | 16.3 s |

The phone read every frame in the first three runs (it missed about a quarter in the last), so the gap is mostly the encoding rather than the camera. UR starts with about a third more fragments because it carries the text token, and a scan that joins mid-animation then needs well over its fragment count: in simulation (200 runs, random join point, no loss) the median was 27 frames for 20 fragments and 123 for 66. The fountain's median was 16 for 15 and 50 for 49.

So about 2x faster on a small token and closer to 3x on a large one, and the gap widens with size. Really nice result.
Item 4: those two vectors came from Cashu-TS, which wrote absent tags as CBOR `undefined`. Fixed in cashubtc/cashu-ts#1428, and #475 regenerates the vectors (checked against CDK and Nutshell).

On the separate question (unknown `nut10` tags), two PRs cover it between them:

- #476 adds the payer rule to NUT-18: a payer locks to every tag in `t`, including ones it does not recognize.
- #474 is the mint side: a secret may carry other NUT-10 tags, and a mint ignores them when evaluating the lock. That is what makes copying an unknown tag safe for the payer.
Item 3: the hash had a stray `a]` prefix. #477 drops it and regenerates the encoded request (checked against CDK and Nutshell). Cashu-TS tests follow in cashubtc/cashu-ts#1430.

Items 1 and 2: #478 brings the NUT-26 text in line with NUT-18. A decoded nostr target is always an `nprofile` (as the vector has it), the table no longer says NIP-04, and the JSON example uses `t`/`a`/`g`.

That gives every item raised here a PR:

- Items 1 and 2: #478
- Item 3: #477
- Item 4: #475
- Unknown `nut10` tags: #476 (payer) and #474 (mint)

This can close once they merge.

Checked on main: the serialized tokens in `00.md` and `tests/00-tests.md` all decode to `"C": "029e8e5050b890a7..."`, matching the JSON examples. The `...505bb890...` value doesn't appear anywhere in the repo history, so this looks like a decoding slip on your side. Closing, but shout if you can reproduce it from a specific line.

Checked on main: the Proof vector verifies with the Carol-side reconstruction as written. The likely culprit is the secret encoding: `x` is the UTF-8 bytes of the 64-character secret string, not the 32 bytes you get from hex-decoding it (see NUT-00). With `Y = hash_to_curve(utf8(secret))` the vector passes; hex-decoding first makes it fail, while every other vector in the file still passes. Closing, but shout if it still fails with that change.

There's no canonical order, and there doesn't need to be: the secret is an opaque string (NUT-00), signed as received (NUT-11), and `C` commits to `hash_to_curve(secret)`, so it can't be re-serialized in any case. A wallet that parses secrets for storage needs to keep a record of the original string alongside. Closing on that basis, but happy to reopen if that doesn't cover the Satocash case.

Thanks for writing this up! This is covered by the Nutroot work for v3 keysets (#443): a NUT-18 request there carries a `nutroot` option where the receiver's key is blinded per NUT-28 on every payment, with a `b` list for any other keys that should be blinded too, and a matching NUT-26 TLV. That gives you the result you describe: one permanent request, every payment locked to a previously unseen key.

With v3 keysets imminent, there are no plans to change legacy P2PK requests right now. Feedback on #443 is very welcome.

Thank you, @robwoodgate. That's every item covered, and quickly.

One small independent check for #475: Nutshell at `11f5c287` decodes both regenerated vectors with no error, and neither transport has a `g` field any more. I didn't check the other PRs.

— Clara

Thanks for the reply. I agree that keeping the bytes you received is the safest thing a wallet can do today. Still, I don't think "`proof.secret` is opaque" settles this. Here is why I think canonical serialization at least deserves a proper pros-and-cons discussion.

**1. A NUT-10 secret isn't opaque. It's structured data stored as a string.**

At the NUT-00 level, `secret` is an arbitrary string that gets hashed to the curve, and there it really is opaque. NUT-10 changes that on purpose. It defines the secret as a JSON array `[kind, {nonce, data, tags}]`, and both sides have to read it:

- The mint has to parse it to enforce spending conditions (pubkeys, `n_sigs`, locktime, refund keys, sigflag).
- The receiving wallet has to parse it to know whether the proof is locked, to which key, and until when.
- Under NUT-11, the signature is computed over the exact serialized string.

So the same data exists twice: as JSON that everyone parses, and as the exact bytes that get signed. Whenever both exist, you have to say which serialization counts. Choosing JSON for the secret already made it non-opaque. The open question is whether the format is pinned down or left to each implementation.

**2. Normalizing JSON before signing or hashing is standard practice.**

Specifying one byte form for JSON that gets signed or hashed is a well-trodden pattern:

- **Nostr (NIP-01)**, in the same ecosystem, defines the event id as the hash of an exactly specified JSON serialization: fixed array order, no whitespace, defined escaping. That's precisely so that any client can rebuild the id from the parsed fields.
- **RFC 8785 (JCS)** exists for exactly this case.
- **Bitcoin** went through the same issue with signatures: BIP-66 made DER encoding strict to remove ambiguity in signature encoding.
- **FIDO2/CTAP2** requires canonical CBOR so that small, constrained authenticators can produce and check exact bytes. That's a close match to the hardware-wallet situation here.

Asking for a canonical form isn't exotic. It's what specs normally do once a serialized structure is covered by a signature.

**3. "Store the string as received" works for software wallets but pushes the cost onto hardware wallets.**

Satocash runs on a JavaCard with a few KB of RAM and limited persistent storage. To verify and sign P2PK proofs safely, the card needs to:

- **Store proofs compactly.** That means a 32-byte nonce, a 33-byte pubkey and a few tag fields, not a variable-length JSON string with arbitrary whitespace and key order. Storing the raw string can cost several times more per proof, which directly limits how many proofs the card can hold.
- **Check what it signs.** Before signing, the card should confirm the secret actually locks to its own key with acceptable tags. If the encoding is canonical, the card can serialize the fields itself and sign bytes it produced, with no general-purpose JSON parser on the card. Without a canonical form, it would have to parse arbitrary JSON (whitespace, key order, escapes, int-vs-string tag values) on a secure element. That's a lot of code and a larger attack surface, in exactly the component that should stay minimal.

The NUT-11 note that "some tag values are int" and that implementations must "cast types appropriately" shows the same ambiguity. One canonical form would resolve that too.

**4. The impact is small, and it can be made backward compatible.**

- **Mints don't need to change.** They keep verifying signatures over the bytes they receive. Nothing in mint verification depends on canonical form.
- **Only the code that creates locked secrets changes.** For most implementations that's a tiny change. CDK's serde output is already compact with fixed field order, and in Python it's mostly a matter of using `json.dumps(..., separators=(",", ":"))` with a fixed key order.
- **No full JCS needed.** NUT-10 content is constrained: hex nonce, hex pubkey, ASCII tag names, numeric values. A small profile is enough: fixed key order (`nonce`, `data`, `tags`), no insignificant whitespace, all tag values as strings, lowercase hex, no escapes.
- **It can be a SHOULD.** Wallets SHOULD create secrets in canonical form. Mints MUST NOT reject non-canonical secrets. Existing tokens stay valid, and constrained devices can refuse or specially handle non-canonical locked proofs they can't safely process.

**5. Side benefit: less wallet fingerprinting.**

Today, whitespace and key order in a locked secret can show which wallet software created it. A canonical form removes that metadata leak at no cost.

**6. The real downsides, for fairness.**

- **Spec churn.** It's one more rule to specify and test, though test vectors make it cheap.
- **Legacy tokens.** Non-canonical tokens already in circulation stay non-canonical. The SHOULD/MUST NOT split above handles that without breaking anything.
- **The robustness principle.** "Be liberal in what you accept" argues against strictness, but the proposal is only strict about what wallets *produce*, not what mints *accept*.

None of these seems to outweigh the benefit of making Cashu P2PK practical on secure hardware, which is where the strongest key custody is.

**Proposal:** add a short "canonical serialization" section to NUT-10 (SHOULD for wallets creating secrets, no new requirement on mints), with the minimal profile above and a few test vectors. I'm happy to draft the PR if there's agreement on the direction.

Thanks for the detailed write-up, the constrained-device case is a fair one.

The direction is to retire the NUT-10 JSON lock family in favor of "Nutroot" secrets with v3 keysets (#443), so there is limited benefit in adding new rules to a soon-deprecated format.

Nutroot should suit Satocash better anyway: the secret is a fixed 33-byte public key, so there is nothing to parse or serialize on the card. 

One thing to check on your side: every v3 input signs the whole transaction, so there is no `SIG_INPUTS` equivalent. This may impact your approach to spending, so a hardware wallet's view on #443 would be welcome.
Thanks for the review @robwoodgate, Updated the option name to `preimage`.

We built an offline signer for SIG_ALL swaps on an ESP32-P4 signing device (KISS Signer): it holds the NUT-13 P2PK keys, a web wallet holds only locked proofs, and they talk by animated QR. Our request format turned out to be nearly the same shape as `sigallA`, so we would rather extend this than define a second one.

The one thing `sigallA` is missing for an offline signer is a way to tell its own change from a payment. Every output is a blinded message, so today a signer can only show the total of all outputs. We added an optional `change` member per output (NUT-13 counter, nonce, blinding factor r): the signer rebuilds the P2PK secret itself, recomputes B_ and refuses a mismatch, then shows "X sat leaving, Y sat coming back". Draft, with the full list of signer checks:
https://github.com/DIYbitcoin/kiss-signer/blob/develop/docs/specs/nut-xx-offline-signer.md

It runs on the device and was tested end to end against testnut. Would you be open to folding the `change` member (and an optional `signer.counter`) into this NUT, or would you prefer it as a follow-on PR?

cashu-ts now reads a null `id` or `memo` in a payment payload as omitted (cashubtc/cashu-ts#1437, v4 backport in cashubtc/cashu-ts#1442). On the receiver question we'd lean to MUST: other languages don't separate null from absent the way JS does, so tolerant receivers are the safer default, with payers SHOULD omit.
